The ?? operator checks with isset() semantics, so undefined variables don't trigger a warning.
PHP's echo construct accepts multiple comma-separated arguments and outputs them in sequence, so 'a' and 'b' are printed together as "ab".
In PHP, `print` is a language construct that returns 1 and, unlike most constructs, can be used within expressions (e.g., `$x = print 'hi';`).
The elvis operator ?: returns its left operand when it is truthy, and its right operand otherwise.
PHP 8 lowered the precedence of the concatenation operator below that of + and - (in PHP 7 they shared the same precedence).
PHP's ** operator is right-associative, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512.
In PHP 8, '.' and '+' have equal precedence and are left-associative, so it evaluates as ('sum: ' . 2) + 3 → 'sum: 2' + 3 → 5.
Strict comparison (===) requires arrays to have the same key/value pairs in the same order with the same types.
0 == false is a loose comparison that returns true, not false; strict comparison would use ===.

In PHP 8, comparison of a non-numeric string with a number no longer casts the string to a number; instead 0 is cast to "0" and compared as strings, so "abc" == 0 is false (this was true only in PHP 7 and earlier).
With loose (==) comparison, null is loosely equal to 0, "", and false in PHP.
PHP's int cast of a string takes the leading numeric part, stopping at the first non-numeric character.
PHP type juggling converts the numeric string '5' to an integer, so 5 + 5 equals 10.
Casting false to string yields an empty string ""; only integer 0 becomes "0".
Floating-point precision makes 0.1 + 0.2 equal 0.30000000000000004, so it is not identical to 0.3.
strrev() reverses bytes, not characters, so it corrupts multi-byte UTF-8 sequences (e.g. 'é' becomes broken bytes).
str_contains returns true because 'Hello world' does contain the substring 'world'.
str_pad() can pad a string on the left, right, or on both sides (STR_PAD_LEFT, STR_PAD_RIGHT, STR_PAD_BOTH).
By default trim() strips spaces as well as tabs, newlines, carriage returns, null bytes, and vertical tabs (its default mask is " \t\n\r\0\x0B").
strlen counts bytes, and 'é' in UTF-8 is 2 bytes, so h(1)+é(2)+l(1)+l(1)+o(1) = 6.
A negative start position counts from the end of the string, so it returns the last 3 characters.
ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character converted to uppercase rather than modifying the original string.
Heredoc (<<<EOT) interpolates variables while nowdoc (<<<'EOT') treats content as a literal string.
sort() reindexes numeric keys, so the original key-to-value association is not preserved.
PHP casts numeric string keys to integers, so '5' is stored as int 5.
in_array() uses loose comparison (==) by default; strict comparison (===) only occurs when the third $strict parameter is set to true.
When no callback is given, array_filter removes elements that evaluate to false, including 0, '', null, false, and [].
By default, array_slice() reindexes numeric keys unless preserve_keys is set to true.

The + operator keeps the left operand's value for the duplicate key 'a', yielding ['a' => 1, 'b' => 2], which has 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 added support for spreading arrays with string keys using the ... operator.
In PHP 8, argument unpacking can be combined with named arguments, e.g. foo(...$args, name: 'x') is valid as long as positional arguments come first.
Anonymous functions don't inherit the parent scope automatically — only superglobals are accessible, all other variables must be imported with the use clause.
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments actually passed to the function, which is 3.
Arrow functions can have a block body containing multiple statements, including expressions.
PHP arrow functions automatically capture outer variables by value at the time the arrow function is created, not by reference or lazily.
A static closure cannot bind $this or any variables from the parent scope, so it does not capture $this.
The closure captures $x by value when it is defined, so it returns the original value 5 even after $x is reassigned to 7.
In weak typing mode PHP performs implicit numeric string-to-int conversion, so "5" is accepted for an int parameter.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing properties to be declared directly in the constructor signature.
The final keyword prevents a method (or class) from being overridden in subclasses.
The final modifier prevents any subclass from overriding the method.
Private properties are only accessible within the defining class, so subclasses cannot access them directly.
Anonymous classes get the internal name 'class@anonymous' followed by a NUL byte, the file path and line number.
Since private parent methods are not inherited, PHP does not enforce compatibility rules when a child declares a method with the same name, so any visibility may be used.
__get() is triggered both for non-existent properties and for existing but inaccessible (private/protected) ones.

PHP throws an Error (e.g. 'Cannot modify readonly property') when assigning to an already initialized readonly property, because it's a fatal language-level violation rather than a catchable application exception.
PHP interfaces can contain constants, which implementing classes inherit automatically.
The instanceof operator returns true if the left operand is an instance of the class or implements the interface named by the right operand.
Since PHP 7.0, interfaces can declare static methods, though they cannot have a body.
The instanceof operator checks both class inheritance and interface implementation, returning true if the object is an instance of the class or implements the interface.
PHP interfaces can only declare method signatures without bodies; only traits (and abstract classes) can provide default implementations.
PHP allows abstract methods to be declared public or protected, though declaring them private is an error.
The cases() method returns an array containing each declared case of the enum, and Foo declares three cases (A, B, C).
PHP 8.2 introduced support for constants declared directly inside traits.
Both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, which defines methods like getMessage(), getCode(), and getTrace().
TypeError extends the Error class, not Exception, so it is not caught by catch (Exception $e).
The @ operator only suppresses error/warning messages, it does not affect exceptions.
intdiv() throws DivisionByZeroError when dividing by zero.
The finally block always executes regardless of whether an exception was caught, thrown, or no exception occurred at all.
An exception thrown in a finally block replaces any return value or exception from the try block and propagates itself.
In PHP, objects are always truthy, so casting an object to bool returns true.
Shutdown functions registered with register_shutdown_function() are executed when the script terminates, including when exit() is called.
A use statement only creates an alias for the namespace and does not trigger loading of the class file; the file is loaded when the class is actually used.
In PHP, `use function Namespace\name;` imports a function, while `use const` imports a constant.
The App\ prefix is stripped and the remaining Controller\Api\UserController is converted to the path Controller/Api/UserController.php under src/.
Composer's generated vendor/autoload.php ultimately calls spl_autoload_register() to register its autoloading functions (e.g., the ClassLoader instance).
__NAMESPACE__ is a magic constant that returns the name of the current namespace as a string (an empty string if in the global namespace).
An unqualified class name in new is resolved relative to the current namespace (falling back to the global namespace only if not found there), not directly from the global root.
PSR-4 strips the namespace prefix App\ and appends the remaining relative path Model\User as src/Model/User.php.

PHP requires import (use) statements in the outermost scope of a file or inside a namespace block — writing one inside a function body produces a parse error, since only closures accept use for variable binding.
In PHP, arrays are value types, so assigning one array to another copies the data unless a reference (&) is used.
PHP arrays are assigned by value, so modifying $b does not affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
PHP functions have their own scope, so variables defined outside must be brought in via the global keyword, $GLOBALS, or passed as arguments (superglobals excepted).
unset($GLOBALS['x']) removes the variable globally, not just from the function's local scope.
inc() takes $n by reference and increments it, so $n becomes 6.
foreach by value iterates over a copy (copy-on-write separation) of the array, so modifications inside the loop don't affect the ongoing pass; only foreach by reference sees live changes.
Static properties belong to the class itself, so all instances share and see the same value.
PHP converts boolean array keys to integers, so true is stored as 1 and false as 0.
PHP 7.0 added Generator::getReturn(), which returns the value passed to return inside a generator.
Calling rewind() on a generator that has already run to completion throws the exception 'Cannot rewind a generator that has already been run'.
yield from passes control and yields values from the inner generator or iterable until it is exhausted.
A function containing yield returns a Generator object, so get_class() yields its class name Generator.
The generator yields from the array [1, 2, 3], producing 3 elements which iterator_to_array collects.
SplStack implements a LIFO (Last In, First Out) stack structure, not a FIFO queue.
ArrayIterator is a built-in PHP class that implements the Iterator interface, allowing arrays to be traversed with foreach and iterator methods.
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate (returning an ArrayIterator), so it can be traversed with foreach.
password_hash() automatically generates a random salt when no salt parameter is provided, making manual salt handling unnecessary.
In PHP 8, PASSWORD_DEFAULT uses bcrypt (with an automatic salt), not md5, which is considered insecure for password hashing.
password_verify returns true because the password matches the generated hash (bcrypt with the default algorithm).
strip_tags() only removes HTML/PHP tags, while SQL injection must be prevented with prepared statements or proper escaping.
session_regenerate_id() creates a new session ID upon login, making it harder for an attacker to exploit a pre-set session ID (session fixation).
php_sapi_name() returns the name of the Server Application Programming Interface (SAPI) currently in use, such as 'cli'.

session_destroy() removes the session data stored on the server but leaves the session cookie in the browser, so you must also delete it (e.g., setcookie() with an expired date) or call session_unset() first.
session_start() must be called before the $_SESSION array becomes available, as it initializes the session.
The array_find() function (along with array_find_key, array_any, and array_all) was introduced in PHP 8.4.
Property hooks (e.g. public string $fullName { get => ...; set => ...; }) were introduced in PHP 8.4 via the Property Hooks RFC.
PHP 8.4 introduced asymmetric visibility, allowing setters to have a different visibility than getters, e.g. public private(set).
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute, which warns when a return value is unused, was introduced in PHP 8.5.
The pipe operator |> was introduced as a new feature in PHP 8.5.
The clone-with syntax clone($obj, ['x' => 1]) was introduced as a new feature in PHP 8.5.
array_first() and array_last() are not native PHP functions; they exist as Laravel collection/helper functions rather than in any PHP version.
The revised Partial Function Application v2 RFC reached the required two-thirds majority during the PHP 8.5 development cycle, making 8.5 the version it was adopted for.
The clamp_v2 RFC introducing the clamp() function was accepted and implemented in the PHP 8.6 release branch.
No such RFC named "Context Managers" has been accepted into PHP as of that date, so the claim is false.
No PHP RFC named "Bound-Erased Generic Types" exists in that timeframe; generics are still unimplemented in PHP.
No accepted RFC exists to enable ZTS (thread safety) by default in PHP; builds still default to non-ZTS.
PHP has never added native generics support, and as of PHP 8.5 parameterized types remain absent, relying on annotations and static analyzers instead.
PHP's yearly November release cycle means 8.5 (Nov 2025) was the current stable on 2026-11-07, with 8.6 still upcoming later that month.
The PHP 6 project, which was to bring native Unicode support, was abandoned, so the release after PHP 5.6 was PHP 7.0.
The #[\Deprecated] attribute RFC was accepted for PHP 8.4, allowing internal functions and userland code to emit deprecation notices via an attribute.
Both clean and onion architecture require that inner layers remain independent of outer layers, with all dependencies pointing inward toward the domain/core.
Domain entities should remain framework-agnostic, depending only on the language and standard library to keep business logic isolated from infrastructure.
Controllers and Twig templates belong to the presentation layer; business logic is implemented in services/use cases which controllers merely invoke.
The innermost layer of the onion architecture holds the domain entities/core business rules.
Tools like Deptrac statically analyze dependencies between layers and can report forbidden calls, which makes CI builds fail when violations occur.
In clean architecture, use cases must not depend on framework or delivery-mechanism concerns like HTTP requests or an EntityManager, so accepting them violates dependency rules.
A repository provides a collection-like interface for accessing aggregates/entities while abstracting the underlying storage mechanism.

In clean architecture, database-specific details live in the outermost infrastructure layer, so replacing PostgreSQL with another RDBMS only affects that layer while the domain and use case layers remain untouched.
In DDD, an aggregate is a cluster of domain objects treated as a consistency boundary, not merely a database table.

In Domain-Driven Design, Value Objects have no identity and are defined solely by their attribute values, so two instances with equal field values are considered equal, and they are kept immutable to preserve that equality.
In Domain-Driven Design, all external access and modifications to an aggregate are routed through its aggregate root, which enforces the invariants.
In DDD, repositories manage whole aggregates through their root entity, keeping consistency boundaries intact rather than exposing individual internal entities.
In Domain-Driven Design, ubiquitous language is a shared language used consistently by both developers and domain experts.
In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context is the boundary within which a model and its ubiquitous language stay consistent, while outside it the same terms refer to different models.
DDD favors a rich domain model where objects encapsulate behavior and invariants, not just data access.
In Domain-Driven Design, a bounded context defines a boundary within which a particular model is defined and consistent, so the same concept is represented by different classes in different contexts.
Symfony services are instantiated eagerly when requested through the container; true lazy loading requires explicitly setting the `lazy: true` option to generate a proxy.
The debug:router command (alias router:debug) lists all registered routes with their methods, patterns, and controllers.
Autowiring automatically resolves constructor dependencies by type hinting, so most services don't need manual declaration.
Twig compiles templates to optimized PHP code and caches the result for subsequent requests.
In dev the kernel only checks file timestamps on each request and re-dumps the container when a tracked config/service file has changed, rather than rebuilding it every time.
Symfony reads the APP_ENV environment variable to determine which environment (e.g. dev or prod) is active.
Symfony can only invoke controller methods that are public, since the controller instance calls them from outside the class.
The EventSubscriberInterface itself grants no priority; ordering depends on explicit priority values and registration order.
The new authenticator-based security system was introduced in Symfony 5.1, and the legacy guard authenticators were deprecated in 5.4 and removed in Symfony 6.0.
The #[IsGranted] attribute (Symfony\Component\Security\Http\Attribute\IsGranted) enforces the given role/ability on a controller method, throwing AccessDeniedException (403) if unmet.
Symfony Security Voters implement VoterInterface and are the mechanism used by the AuthorizationChecker's isGranted() method to determine access to specific objects.
Doctrine annotation support was removed in Symfony 6.0, so in Symfony 7+ only PHP attributes (#[Assert\...]) are supported for declaring validation constraints.
Symfony enables CSRF protection for forms by default, and validation of the token occurs automatically when the form is submitted.
Symfony forms are always validated server-side, since client-side HTML5 checks can be bypassed or are only a UX convenience.
The Symfony Maker bundle command 'make:form' generates a new FormType class.

Before the security token is serialized into the session, Symfony calls eraseCredentials(), which strips the plain-text password from the token/user, so only non-sensitive data (e.g. the password hash) is ever persisted.
In Symfony, bundles' configuration files are placed in config/packages, with each file dedicated to a specific bundle or topic (e.g., framework.yaml, security.yaml).
This is a common convention where the tracked .env holds safe defaults and the gitignored .env.local holds machine-specific secrets.
The debug:container command lists all registered services and their aliases in the Symfony service container.

ContainerInterface::setParameter() is a public method that writes to the in-memory parameter bag, so it works from a controller (though it only affects the current request and not services that already read the parameter).
Since Symfony 3.4, services are private by default, so you must explicitly declare them public to fetch them directly from the container.
Most bundles ship with sensible default configuration and work without any config file; config is optional, not mandatory.
Symfony's dependency injection container supports the %env(VAR)% placeholder syntax in configuration files like services.yaml to read environment variable values.
The APP_DEBUG environment variable controls whether Symfony runs in debug mode, enabling the profiler and Twig debug features.
In Symfony Messenger, a single message can be handled by multiple handlers registered for that message class.
The sync transport handles the message immediately in the same process instead of queueing it for an async worker.
In Symfony, the messenger:consume console command starts a worker that processes queued messages.
In Symfony Messenger, the retry_strategy (with max_retries, delay, etc.) is configured at the transport level, not globally for the messenger.
By default Messenger uses the PhpSerializer (PHP's native serialize()), and JSON serialization must be explicitly configured.
Symfony Scheduler schedules messages with recurrence triggers and dispatches them via the Messenger bus.
Symfony Messenger's built-in doctrine transport persists messages to database tables using Doctrine DBAL.
Symfony Messenger buses let you register custom middleware and order them relative to the built-in ones using the before/after options.
Symfony follows this schedule: major releases (X.0) every two years in November, with minor releases every six months in May and November.
Symfony 8.x requires PHP 8.4 or higher to run.
Symfony 7.0 removed support for Doctrine docblock annotations in favor of PHP 8 attributes, which are now the only option for routes, validation, etc.
Symfony's AssetMapper component maps imported CSS/JS files via an importmap.php configuration, eliminating the need for Node.js or webpack.
Symfony 6.4 is a long-term support (LTS) release with extended maintenance until 2027.
Symfony's policy is that features deprecated in one major version are removed in the next major release, so major releases do remove them.
Symfony ships UPGRADE-*.md files in its repository documenting breaking changes for each version transition.
Symfony's AssetMapper component maps and serves assets directly from PHP and generates the importmap, removing the need for Node.js, npm or Webpack.
Symfony releases minor versions in May and November, so 8.2 would come at the end of November 2026, after 2026-11-07.
Symfony releases majors every two years in November and minor versions every six months, so 8.0 (Nov 2025) → 8.1 (May 2026) → 8.2 (Nov 2026).
Symfony releases minor versions in May and November, so the version following 8.1 (May 2026) is 8.2 (November 2026).
8.2 would be a minor release, which follows backward compatibility promises and does not require rewriting applications for new APIs.
PHP follows semantic versioning within a major branch, so 8.x minor releases guarantee backward compatibility (only deprecations may be added, not breaking changes).
Following Symfony's release cycle (x.0 in November, then x.1–x.4 with the final minor and the next major released two years later), 8.4 is the last minor of the 8.x branch before 9.0.
Symfony 8.x (including 8.2) sets its minimum at PHP 8.4, and minor releases within a major don't raise the PHP requirement to a new PHP version like 8.5.
Symfony's backward compatibility policy states that code deprecated in a given major version (8.x) is only removed in the next major release (9.0).
Twig's {{ }} only evaluates Twig expressions through its own template engine, not arbitrary PHP code.
Twig enables the autoescape option by default (using the 'html' strategy), so `{{ var }}` output is escaped unless you use the raw filter or explicitly disable it.
The |e filter (alias of escape) defaults to the 'html' escaping strategy, encoding characters like <, >, &, ", ' for safe HTML output.
The format_number filter from twig/intl-extra formats a number according to a given locale.
The |raw filter marks a value as safe, telling Twig not to HTML-escape it when outputting.
Twig uses {{ }} for printing expression values and {% %} for control tags like if, for, and set.
Twig allows declaring variables with the {% set %} tag, and values can also come from other sources like expressions and macros.
The dump() function outputs the debug structure of a variable, similar to var_dump() in PHP.
Bootstrap is a front-end CSS/JavaScript library providing ready-made UI components (buttons, modals, grids), not a single-page application framework like React or Angular.
The .container class sets a fixed max-width that changes at each Bootstrap breakpoint, unlike .container-fluid which is always 100% wide.
The Bootstrap grid is built on CSS floats but uses 12 columns per row, not 16.
Bootstrap 5 defines exactly five named breakpoints — sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl — with xs being the default (no infix) rather than a named breakpoint.
In Bootstrap, spacing utilities are generated from the $spacer variable, so .mt-3 equals 3 × $spacer and .px-2 equals 2 × $spacer on each side.
Bootstrap 5 uses the data-bs-toggle attribute (e.g. data-bs-toggle="dropdown") to activate interactive components.
Bootstrap 5 removed jQuery as a dependency and components are implemented in vanilla JavaScript.
In Bootstrap 5.3, dark mode is enabled with the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute on the root element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM never auto-creates tables at runtime; schema must be created explicitly via commands like doctrine:schema:create or migrations.
persist() schedules a new entity for insertion, making it managed, but no SQL is executed until flush() is called.
EntityManager::merge() was removed in Doctrine ORM 3.0, so it no longer exists.
DQL is an object-oriented query language that operates on entity classes and their properties, abstracting away the underlying database tables and columns.
Eloquent's find() method returns null when no matching record is found.
Doctrine requires an explicit call to EntityManager::flush(); there is no automatic flush at the end of a request.
Managed entities are already tracked by the Unit of Work, so flush() detects and commits property changes via change tracking without needing persist().
In Doctrine ORM, remove() only schedules the entity for deletion; the actual DELETE SQL is executed when flush() is called.
MVCC allows readers and writers to operate concurrently without blocking each other, since each transaction sees a snapshot of the data.
The EXPLAIN command displays the execution plan for a query without running it.
SERIAL creates an implicit sequence default and its column can still be updated, while GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY is a SQL-standard, non-updatable identity mechanism, so they behave differently.
In PostgreSQL, a UNIQUE constraint treats NULLs as distinct, so multiple rows with NULL are allowed by default (unlike some other databases).
string_agg(value, delimiter) is the PostgreSQL aggregate that concatenates string values using a specified separator.
Plain VACUUM only marks dead-tuple space as reusable within the table; only VACUUM FULL (or table rewrite) returns space to the OS.
The PARTITION BY clause divides result rows into groups over which the window function is computed independently.
READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads, not non-repeatable reads, which require REPEATABLE READ or higher isolation.
In PostgreSQL's default autocommit mode, each statement is executed within its own implicit transaction that commits automatically on success.
COMMIT ends the current transaction and permanently saves all changes made within it.
UPDATE and DELETE must first locate matching rows, and an index speeds up that lookup just as it does for SELECT.
PostgreSQL supports SAVEPOINT to create rollback points, allowing partial rollback of statements within a transaction using ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and reports real execution statistics, unlike plain EXPLAIN which only shows the plan.
pgvector is the PostgreSQL extension that adds the vector data type and similarity search indexes (like HNSW and IVFFlat) for embeddings.
A partial index includes only rows that match the WHERE condition, making it smaller and faster for queries that use the same condition.
PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which tracks predicate/range locks rather than locking the rows read.
HTTP status code 201 is 'Created', which indicates that the request succeeded and resulted in a new resource being created.
204 No Content indicates the request succeeded but the server returns no response body, which is typical after a DELETE.
The HTTP specification classifies DELETE as idempotent, since repeating it leaves the resource in the same (deleted/404) state.
The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is sent by the server in its response, not by the client; the client only sends the Origin header.
HTTP status 429 "Too Many Requests" is returned when a client has sent more requests in a given amount of time than the rate limit allows.
The opposite is true: 4xx codes indicate client errors, while 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.
The Content-Type header specifies the media type (MIME type) of the request or response body, while Content-Encoding describes the encoding.
RFC 5789 states that PATCH, unlike PUT (which must be idempotent), is not required to be idempotent, since applying the same patch twice may be invalid or unintended.
A plain == comparison is vulnerable to timing attacks (and potential type juggling), so you should use hash_equals() instead.
CSRF tokens are generated by the server, tied to the user's session, and validated server-side before processing unsafe (state-changing) requests like POST.
The Content-Security-Policy HTTP response header is used to enable and configure a site's CSP policy.
OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, not an authentication protocol; the access token grants access to resources rather than identifying the user (that's the role of OpenID Connect's ID token).
XSS is primarily prevented by output encoding/escaping data when rendering it, not solely by input validation, which cannot catch every malicious payload.
In the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, the authorization server redirects to redirect_uri with a code parameter, which the client exchanges for an access token at the token endpoint.
Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials used to obtain new access tokens without re-authenticating the user.
A salt does not need to be secret; it is typically stored alongside the hash and its purpose is to prevent rainbow table attacks, not to provide secrecy.
PHPUnit only discovers and runs test methods in classes that extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase (or a custom base class extending it).
In PHPUnit, setUp() runs before each test method; setUpBeforeClass() is the method that runs once before all tests in the class.
A data provider supplies multiple sets of arguments so the test runs once per dataset, not exactly once.
expectException($exceptionClass) is the PHPUnit method used to declare that a test expects an exception of the given class to be thrown.
The opposite is true: mocks verify which methods were called and how they were called, while stubs only return canned data.
PHPUnit 10 deprecated doc-comment annotations in favor of attributes such as #[DataProvider] for supplying test data.
PHPUnit requires tests to be independent and isolated, providing no built-in mechanism for one test to depend on another's results.
PHPUnit's --order-by=random option randomizes the execution order of test cases.
